It's an increasingly common take that AI hacking means cybersecurity is doomed.

I disagree. I think cybersecurity is naturally defense-favoring once people get their shit together. And anyone who continues to hold cryptocurrency (including me, ~90% of my net worth) is implicitly making that bet.

Here's why I am making that bet.

First, the oversimplified punchy one-line statement:

If AI can prove Navier-Stokes and FLT, then AI can prove the statement "this program is secure" as a mathematical theorem. Even if the program is very complicated.

Now, the nuance:

(See also: https://vitalik.eth.limo/general/2026/05/18/fv.html )

The word "secure" is hiding all kinds of skeletons in the closet in terms of what it actually means. What does it mean for Signal (the encrypted messenger) to be "secure"?

The most basic definition you might think of is: no one who doesn't hold the recipient's secret key can read the contents of the message.

But:

* Did you remember to include _other_ critical forms of security? Can the adversary forge messages? Can the attacker prevent messages from reaching the recipient? Can they cause your client to crash by sending malformed messages?
* Have you made sure that your model of the adversary includes attackers that interfere with the protocol actively and not just passively? And attackers that interfere by replaying messages to you or the recipient that either of you sent over the wire at any point earlier?
* What if the adversary hacked (or _is_) the Signal server?
* How did you learn which public key belongs to the recipient in the first place? What if that process was tampered with?
* What if your device gets hacked at some point in the past or future - is your message still safe then?
* What if your key leaks because of a bug in your operating system? Or because you got a bugged version of the Signal client? Or what if the database is corrupted?
* Or the libraries, interpreter or compiler of the programming language you wrote it in?
* What if your key leaks because tiny perturbations in perceptible signals generated by the hardware leak mathematical relationships that can extract the key a few hundredths of a bit at a time?
* Are you hiding the *size* of the payload? Does that matter?
* You're definitely not hiding the identity of the sender and the recipient, and the exact time each message was sent (think: not just time-of-day, but also time deltas between one message and the next). Is that not enough to deduce a lot of important facts about what relationships you have, and what *kinds* of conversations you are having?

So ... even definitions can be over a thousand lines of code, and need deep careful thought to figure them out.

Working on making definitions more human-readable is of extreme importance - it's perhaps the only "high-level language" that matters right now.

But even still, even despite all of the above, for security-critical components, the definition is a much smaller attack surface than the implementation. Verifying that the definition is adequate is a much more tractable task than scanning over the code directly - and can become even more tractable with better tooling.

Definitions are also _additive_: if two groups have two different definitions A and B, then, well, you can just prove that the program satisfies both A and B. Code is not additive in this way: if a program is A + B, a bug in A _or_ B can sink the whole thing. Definitions are additive. And if you can't satisfy A and B at the same time, you've isolated the most important philosophical issue for your project to spend its next few weeks grappling with.

Sometimes, definitions are not much smaller than the implementation - UI components might be one example. But for many of the most critical components - message-passing protocols, sandboxes, cryptography like SNARKs and FHE - the asymmetry is real.

Historically, a large class of failures with this approach have come from people only verifying a small portion of their code, that they self-declared to be the security-critical portion, and ignoring the rest - and it turns out that something in the rest of the code is security-critical too.

This was reasonable back when verification was difficult and scarce. The solution today: sorry, you have to verify over literally your entire program, including database, networking, any caching layers, everything. Modern AI can do it.

So it's not about "the good guys find all the vulnerabilities before the bad guys do" - that could maybe work too, after all a finite program only has a finite number of vulns, but it's riskier - it's specifically an asymmetric strategy of making code that is much more resilient in the first place.

This is the kind of direction that Ethereum is going in for the next few years. There is no future for blockchains - especially blockchains with scalability and privacy - without doing this. We need to make software actually secure. And we have already made a lot of progress.

Vitalik is making the right bet on formal methods, but “cybersecurity is naturally defense-favoring” is too fat a claim

@VitalikButerin 

FLT and Navier-Stokes are closed statements inside a formal system. “This program is secure” is not. That claim is about hardware, compilers, OS, networks, keys, people, and economics. An AI that can formalize known math still has not closed a threat model

The bottleneck is no longer the proof. It is the spec. The tweet itself shows this

“Secure” for Signal balloons into a thousand caveats and is still leaky. Proving P satisfies Spec is cheaper than making Spec match the security you actually need

An incomplete spec plus a perfect proof is just a certified hole. Spec elicitation is still the weakest part of the AI stack

Definitions are additive only inside one model. A and B work together if both teams are formalizing the same environment. In practice one group covers crypto, another covers the protocol, and someone forgets replay, side channels, PKI, UI, and metadata. Two “correct” specs can both check out and both be insufficient

The TCB does not disappear. It just moves

A full proof of the client still leaves the prover kernel, the compiler, Spectre-class CPUs, microcode, the runtime, updates, the supply chain, and the operator. “Proved in Lean” is not the same as “you cannot derive falsehood from this system” 

Defense only wins if the TCB itself gets smaller and verified. That is a harder and more expensive program

The attacker gets the same AI. Defense proves one property against one model

Offense looks for everything left outside it: MEV, governance, bridges, frontends, timing, hardware, social engineering, update bugs. A finite number of bugs in a finite program is a weak argument if the real holes live at the seams

Where the thesis is strong: crypto primitives, sandboxes, consensus, SNARKs, FHE, ZK-EVMs, message-passing. There the spec is smaller than the implementation, the properties are stable, formal methods already work, and AI actually cheapens proofs. For Ethereum that is the right vector

Where it is weak: holding crypto is not the same as betting that cybersecurity as a whole tilts toward defense. Crypto is still alive because attacks are expensive, clients are diverse, audits and bounties exist, and the design stayed conservative

Not because the whole stack is provably secure. User keys, bridges, frontends, and L2 operators remain offense-favoring

Formal verification plus AI is the best known way to make critical components harder. It does not make cybersecurity naturally defense-favoring. The winner is not whoever can prove anything against a sloppy spec. It is whoever writes the right definitions and shrinks the TCB

Since many people are learning about effective altruism, it's worth learning about Mozi, the ancient Chinese philosopher who was surprisingly close to being a proto-effective-altruist (particularly the global-health-focused variety, not the AI-risk-focused variety).

He valued the twin goals of (i) universal love, loving everyone and not just yourself and people similar or close to you, and (ii) being efficient about how you use your limited resources to most effectively help people.

https://ctext.org/mozi
AI on how Mozi would feel about modern effective altruism - the similarities and the differences (especially with the AI-risk-focused variety)

Mozi is also surprisingly proto d/acc (!!)

Books 14 and 15 are basically open-source city defense manuals (though the idea transmission was a distributed process, it was not one guy writing a great tome and then everyone else copying and reading it)

https://ctext.org/mozi/book-14

The explicit goal was to upgrade people's knowledge of defensive arts, and thus shift the offense/defense balance further toward defense.

Defense is central to his thinking. Offensive war is the primary example of behavior that causes a small benefit to perpetrators at the expense of a large cost to victims, and it's also the primary example of why it really is best to love everyone universally, and not just love people inside your own country - if you do the latter, you might think it's a good idea to make your country wealthier and safer by making other countries poorer and less safe, but ultimately if everyone does that then everyone is worse off.

Yeah we pretty much have to do the hard thing, and push the "open source, secure and verifiable" paradigm up and down the full stack, including operating systems and including hardware.

Fatalism that the hardware layer has fifteen skeletons in the closet that nobody can understand is a thing that has to be challenged, attacked and overturned explicitly.

text:
Here's my conversation with Andrew Scull, all about psychiatry, its long history from Freud/Jung to today, including asylums, icepick lobotomies, electroshock therapy, antidepressants, antipsychotics, and some horrific treatments that were considered mainstream where doctors injected patients with malaria, induced insulin comas, and pulled out their teeth, all in the name of curing madness.

There are a lot of lessons to learn from history here. One of the most important for me is just how incredibly complex the human mind is, and how hard the task is of understanding & treating the nearly infinite ways it can stumble/faulter.

Humans are amazing. In part, because our minds are such a damn complicated mess.

It's here on X in full and is up everywhere else (see comment).

We're sharing our new framework for tracking, investigating, and disclosing instances of model misalignment at OpenAI.

The framework sets criteria and timelines for public disclosure, including when we haven’t yet fully explained or mitigated the behavior. More complex cases may require longer investigation or coordination with third parties.

We’ll prioritize examples that reveal new misalignment mechanisms, meaningful changes in known behavior, or findings that challenge assumptions about safety or mitigation.

Alongside the framework, we’re publishing six reports on instances of misaligned behavior we’ve observed during the training or evaluation of our models in the last six months.

This is a starting point. We’ll refine the process through experience and public feedback, and share more reports on an ongoing basis.

https://openai.com/index/model-misalignment-reporting-framework/
